# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

evidence.subject: fix: use first-parent traversal in explain to handle merge commits
evidence.body:
repo.Log() does a full DAG walk, following ALL parents of merge commits.
When main is merged into a feature branch, this walks into main's entire
history. The consecutiveMainLimit (100) would fire before older feature
branch checkpoints were found, silently dropping them.

Replace repo.Log() with a walkFirstParentCommits helper that follows only
first parents, naturally staying on the feature branch's commit chain.
This simplifies getBranchCheckpoints, getAssociatedCommits, and
isShadowBranchReachable by removing the reachableFromMain precomputation
and consecutiveMainLimit tracking.

# Fix `entire explain` branch filtering with merge commits

## Context

`entire explain` branch filtering breaks when a feature branch has merge commits from main. The root cause: `repo.Log()` with `git.LogOrderCommitterTime` traverses ALL parents of merge commits (full DAG walk). After merging main into a feature branch, the walker enters main's full history. The `consecutiveMainLimit` (100) fires before older feature branch checkpoints are found, silently dropping them.

go-git v5's `LogOptions` has no `FirstParent` option, so we need manual first-parent traversal.

## Changes

### 1. Extract first-parent walk helper in `explain.go`

Create a `walkFirstParentCommits` helper that walks the first-parent chain from a starting hash, calling a visitor function f

evidence.subject: Replace O(N) FlattenTree+BuildTreeFromEntries with O(depth) tree surgery for metadata branch
evidence.body:
WriteCommitted, UpdateCommitted, and UpdateSummary previously flattened the
entire metadata branch tree into a map and rebuilt it from scratch on every
write. This was O(total checkpoints) and became the dominant bottleneck as
checkpoint count grew.

New approach: read only the target checkpoint's subtree, modify it, build a
small subtree, and splice it into the root tree using UpdateSubtree — touching
only the 2-level shard path while preserving all sibling hashes.

Benchstat (ManyPriorCheckpoints, 200 existing checkpoints):
  sec/op:    109ms → 7.7ms   (-93%)
  B/op:      6.3MB → 2.1MB   (-66%)
  allocs/op: 75k   → 12k     (-84%)

evidence.subject: Adapt to Codex 0.129's renamed hooks feature flag and trust gate
evidence.body:
Codex 0.129 surfaces two warnings on every startup against entire's
existing hook installation:

  ⚠ \`[features].codex_hooks\` is deprecated. Use \`[features].hooks\` instead.
  ⚠ N hooks need review before they can run. Open /hooks to review them.

The first is a feature-flag rename (codex-rs PR #20522): \`codex_hooks\`
is still accepted as a legacy alias but emits a deprecation warning.
ensureProjectFeatureEnabled now writes the new \`hooks = true\` form and
rewrites any existing \`codex_hooks = true\` line on next install so the
warning stops firing without touching the user's config by hand. The
existing/legacy detection uses an exact line match — \`hooks = true\` is
a substring of \`codex_hooks = true\`, so a naive Contains() would treat
the legacy form as if the new form was already present.

The second is Codex 0.129's per-user hook trust gate (codex-rs PR
#20321). Unmanaged hooks defined in .codex/hooks.json don't run until
the user has approved the current hash via /hooks once. Pre-trusting on
install would mean replicating Codex's NormalizedHookIdentity →
canonical-JSON → SHA256 hash and writing trusted_hash entries to the
user's ~/.codex/config.toml — fragile and invasive. Print a one-time
hint after a Codex install instead, pointing the user at /hooks.

Adds TestInstallHooks_RewritesLegacyFeatureLine pinning the legacy →
canonical rewrite. Updates the e2e Codex seed to use the new form.

evidence.subject: Fix Cursor session mis-identified as Claude Code
evidence.body:
When Cursor IDE forwards a single user prompt to both .cursor/hooks.json
and .claude/settings.json, two `entire` hook processes race to claim the
session and the loser's wrong agent_type can win the last write.

Three layered defenses:
- SessionStart hint: first agent to fire claims the session ID
  (`<sessionID>.agent` written with O_EXCL).
- Transcript-path override: a transcript inside an agent's session dir
  is authoritative — overrides both hint and the firing hook.
- Per-session file lock: serializes concurrent InitializeSession calls
  so the runner-up takes the cheap update path (`correctSessionAgentType`)
  instead of also creating-from-scratch. Lock files live under
  `<git-common-dir>/entire-locks/` to keep `entire-sessions/` clean.

which hook came from where.

Reaching the SessionStart hook handler proves SessionStart is itself
trusted, so it's the right place to add a contextual nudge: if any
other event we declared in .codex/hooks.json lacks a state entry under
the same hooks-file path, append a one-liner naming the missing events
to the welcome message.

Detection is structural — we read the user's config.toml and look for
\`[hooks.state."<hooks.json>:<event>:<group>:<handler>"]\` headers, no
hash recomputation. That misses the "command changed, hash mismatched"
case (status = Modified), but Codex's own warning still surfaces it,
so we don't need to. The check stays cheap and free of the brittle
hash-replication coupling we declined for production pre-trust.

Codex-only: other agents don't have a per-user trust gate.

evidence.subject: Funnel all session-state mutations through MutateSessionState
evidence.body:
The previous PostToolUse-only lock fixed parallel PostToolUse races but
left every other writer (TurnEnd, PostCommit, condense, model update,
review env adoption, attribution divergence, post-rewrite remap, etc.)
doing its own unlocked load → mutate → save. A PostToolUse save could
still revert Phase, CheckpointTranscriptStart, TurnCheckpointIDs, token
usage, and other fields if it landed between another writer's load and
save.

Convert every session-state load-modify-save in the lifecycle dispatcher
and strategy package to MutateSessionState (or, for the rare new-state
case, to wrap the lone save in acquireSessionGate). The helper now:
  - Takes an OS flock against .git/entire-session-locks/<id>.lock for
    the duration of the load + fn + save.
  - Layers a per-process gate keyed by goroutine ID over the flock so
    nested calls in the same goroutine share the outer's state pointer
    rather than deadlocking on a second flock or losing inner updates
    to the outer save.
  - Returns ErrStateNotFound when no state file exists, letting callers
    distinguish "no session" from a successful no-op.
  - Honours ErrMutationSkip so fn can decline to save when the merge
    produced no change (key for the PostToolUse hot path).

Lock files moved out of .git/entire-sessions/ so callers that enumerate
session state (tests, doctor, status) don't have to filter them.
ClearSessionState sweeps the lock too.

Adds TestMutateSessionState_NestedCallsAreReentrant to lock in the
nested-cal

evidence.subject: Replace O(N) FlattenTree+BuildTreeFromEntries with O(depth) tree surgery for metadata branch
evidence.body:
WriteCommitted, UpdateCommitted, and UpdateSummary previously flattened the
entire metadata branch tree into a map and rebuilt it from scratch on every
write. This was O(total checkpoints) and became the dominant bottleneck as
checkpoint count grew.

New approach: read only the target checkpoint's subtree, modify it, build a
small subtree, and splice it into the root tree using UpdateSubtree — touching
only the 2-level shard path while preserving all sibling hashes.

Benchstat (ManyPriorCheckpoints, 200 existing checkpoints):
  sec/op:    109ms → 7.7ms   (-93%)
  B/op:      6.3MB → 2.1MB   (-66%)
  allocs/op: 75k   → 12k     (-84%)

evidence.subject: attribution: scope Mixed to the touching session and unify authorship rule
evidence.body:
Two related correctness bugs in line attribution:

1. `entire blame` and `entire why` disagreed on the tag. resolveLine marks a
   line [MX] only when its *preferred* candidate is mixed, but the why-time
   enrichment path (enrichAttributionLineWithFetch) marked it [MX] if *any*
   candidate was mixed. A line with a non-mixed preferred candidate and a mixed
   secondary one rendered [AI] in blame and [MX] in why. Extract a single
   authorshipForPreferred() rule used by both paths.

2. Mixed was checkpoint-scoped, not session-scoped. readCheckpointContext
   OR-combined the checkpoint-wide CombinedAttribution with every session's
   attribution, so a line from an agent-only file got tagged [MX] whenever the
   checkpoint *also* touched a hand-edited file. Scope Mixed to the session
   whose work actually touched this file; fall back to the checkpoint-wide
   attribution only when no session metadata resolves.

checkpoint's combined attribution is mixed — the line must stay [AI].

evidence.subject: git: open repositories with alternates-aware storage
evidence.body:
Shared clones can store required objects only through .git/objects/info/alternates. Several checkpoint paths opened repositories with plain go-git storage, so local-only checkpoint commits reachable through alternates could look missing. That made metadata rebase and push paths silently skip checkpoint data and leave remote checkpoint branches incomplete.

Add a gitrepo package that centralizes repository opening, resolves linked worktree .git/commondir layouts, and wires go-git's AlternatesFS so multiple and nested alternates are readable. Route repository openings across the CLI and shared test harnesses through that package so go-git sees the same object graph everywhere.

Also close repository handles after use. Upstream go-git requires callers to close repositories to release filesystem storage resources, so the shared opener documents ownership and call sites now defer Close or register test cleanup.

evidence.subject: Recover a diverged checkpoint ref by fetch+replay instead of leaving it queued
evidence.body:
Build on the non-force push: when a per-checkpoint ref is rejected (it diverged
on the remote — the same checkpoint re-written elsewhere), instead of just
leaving it queued, fetch the remote ref and replay the local-only commits on top
via the existing fetchAndRebaseRefCommon, then retry. The retry stays non-force
(after the replay the local ref is a fast-forward over the remote), so the
remote's commit is preserved as an ancestor, never overwritten. The cherry-pick
is delta-based, so non-overlapping changes merge; a genuine overlap (both sides
rewrote the same file) surfaces as a rebase error and the ref is left for a later
pre-push — degrading to the previous safe behavior, never to a force overwrite.

pre-push keeps the batch push as the fast path (one round-trip when everything
fast-forwards) and falls back to this per-ref recovery only for rejected refs,
removing from the queue just those that land. Adds a test proving a diverged ref
ends up with both the remote-only and local-only changes after recovery.

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

repo.Log() does a full DAG walk, following ALL parents of merge commits.
When main is merged into a feature branch, this walks into main's entire

and consecutiveMainLimit tracking.

evidence.body:
Break the single coarse push_checkpoints_branch span into nested child
spans so `entire doctor trace --hook pre-push` shows where time goes
during a slow checkpoint push instead of one opaque total:

steps nest correctly. Instrumentation only; no behavior change.

evidence.subject: Skip pre-push hook on bootstrap's initial push
evidence.body:
`gh repo create --push` invoked the newly installed `pre-push` hook,
which pushed `entire/checkpoints/v1` alongside the default branch.
GitHub then picked `entire/checkpoints/v1` as the repository's default
branch because it was one of the refs in the initial push.

`git push --no-verify -u origin HEAD`. `--no-verify` bypasses the
pre-push hook for this one push; the checkpoint branch is skipped,
which is safe because a fresh repo has no sessions to checkpoint yet.
Subsequent pushes still go through the hook normally.

Verified against a real GitHub repo: only `main` lands on the remote,
and GitHub's default branch is `main`.

evidence.subject: perf: use worktree.Status() instead of filesystem walk for first checkpoint
evidence.body:
Replace collectWorkingDirectoryFiles() with collectChangedFiles() to fix
slow shadow branch creation when node_modules/ or .worktrees/ exist.

The old implementation walked the entire filesystem, only skipping .git/
and .entire/ directories. This was extremely slow in repos with large
ignored directories like node_modules/ (50k+ files).

The new implementation uses worktree.Status() which:
- Respects .gitignore (excludes node_modules/, build/, etc.)
- Only returns changed files (modified tracked + untracked non-ignored)
- Is much faster: O(changed files) vs O(all files)

The base tree from HEAD already contains all unchanged tracked files,
so we only need to capture files that have changed.

Added tests to verify:
- Modified tracked files are captured (user's uncommitted work)
- Untracked non-ignored files are captured
- Gitignored files are excluded
- Both user and agent changes are captured together

evidence.subject: Add `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints` (git-branch → git-refs)
evidence.body:
Convert checkpoints on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch into per-checkpoint refs
(refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>), the git-refs store's layout.

checkpoint.MigrateBranchToRefs walks the v1 branch tip and, for each checkpoint,
wraps its CURRENT subtree object in a fresh commit and points the ref at it —
existing branch commits are not remapped. Since the git-refs ref tree is the
branch's <shard>/<id> subtree byte-for-byte, a migrated checkpoint reads
identically under either backend. It is idempotent: a checkpoint whose ref
already carries the same tree is skipped, and a changed checkpoint re-migrates by
fast-forward (new commit parents on the existing ref, so no history is lost).
New/advanced refs are enqueued for push; the function itself never pushes.

The `doctor migrate-checkpoints` command reports migrated/skipped/total and, per
the requested policy, only pushes when it can prompt: interactively it asks
whether to push now; non-interactively it never pushes (refs stay queued and
flush on the next push once git-refs is primary). `--dry-run` reports what would
change without writing refs.

Push reuse: the git-refs pre-push queue-flush is extracted into
strategy.flushCheckpointRefsQueue (shared by the fail-soft pre-push path and the
new error-surfacing strategy.PushMigratedCheckpointRefs), so the "push now"
option goes through the exact same fast-forward + fetch/replay logic.

evidence.subject: Funnel all session-state mutations through MutateSessionState
evidence.body:
The previous PostToolUse-only lock fixed parallel PostToolUse races but
left every other writer (TurnEnd, PostCommit, condense, model update,
review env adoption, attribution divergence, post-rewrite remap, etc.)
doing its own unlocked load → mutate → save. A PostToolUse save could
still revert Phase, CheckpointTranscriptStart, TurnCheckpointIDs, token
usage, and other fields if it landed between another writer's load and
save.

Convert every session-state load-modify-save in the lifecycle dispatcher
and strategy package to MutateSessionState (or, for the rare new-state
case, to wrap the lone save in acquireSessionGate). The helper now:
  - Takes an OS flock against .git/entire-session-locks/<id>.lock for
    the duration of the load + fn + save.
  - Layers a per-process gate keyed by goroutine ID over the flock so
    nested calls in the same goroutine share the outer's state pointer
    rather than deadlocking on a second flock or losing inner updates
    to the outer save.
  - Returns ErrStateNotFound when no state file exists, letting callers
    distinguish "no session" from a successful no-op.
  - Honours ErrMutationSkip so fn can decline to save when the merge
    produced no change (key for the PostToolUse hot path).

Lock files moved out of .git/entire-sessions/ so callers that enumerate
session state (tests, doctor, status) don't have to filter them.
ClearSessionState sweeps the lock too.

Adds TestMutateSessionState_NestedCallsAreReentrant to lock in the
nested-cal

evidence.subject: fix(cli): make explain work against checkpoint_remote with partial-clone
evidence.body:
`entire explain <checkpoint-id>` failed with "no checkpoint or commit
found" when the metadata branch was on a configured `checkpoint_remote`
but blobs hadn't been fetched yet. Three coordinated fixes:

1. v1Store now has a blob fetcher configured (the piece resume already
   had via SetBlobFetcher). Without it, go-git's Tree.File() returns
   ErrFileNotFound on a missing blob, which ReadCommitted translates to
   ErrCheckpointNotFound — making it look like the checkpoint doesn't
   exist when really only the blob is absent.

2. FetchBlobs now uses `git fetch-pack` instead of porcelain
   `git fetch`. Porcelain enforces partial-clone integrity checks that
   reject blob-only responses with "did not send all necessary objects",
   so `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` always failed against GitHub for
   repos with filtered_fetches enabled. Plumbing skips those checks and
   just downloads the requested objects.

3. FetchingTree.File now tries `git cat-file` BEFORE the network fetch.
   In partial-clone repos a blob is commonly on disk but invisible to
   go-git's storer (filtered out, or in a packfile not in the cached
   index). Without the short-circuit, every File() burned a network
   round-trip on already-local data — which compounded into per-File
   25s SSH-handshake-and-rejection delays before this fix.

The matching empty-list fetch chain for explain now mirrors

evidence.subject: Fetch missing git-refs checkpoints on demand for reads
evidence.body:
A git-refs primary previously read only checkpoint refs already present locally,
so checkpoints written on another machine (or not yet fetched after clone) read
as not-found. FetchCheckpointRef fetches one ref via the checkpoint remote into
the local ref of the same name; it's wired into the read commands that already
inject FetchBlobsByHash (resume, explain, attribution, tokens profile) via the
new OpenOptions.RefFetcher. gitRefsStore.resolveRefMaybeFetch invokes it once on
a local miss and retries; a failed fetch resolves to ErrCheckpointNotFound. The
git-branch backend ignores it; strategy-side Opens (condensation/rewind) read
just-written local refs and pass no fetcher.

evidence.subject: Add git-refs per-checkpoint checkpoint backend
evidence.body:
Second slice of #1471: a git-backed store that keeps one commit per
refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id> (tree root = checkpoint contents), sharing
the treeWriter subtree core with the git-branch store.

  (orphan-then-parented history, stamps refs-v1, no Vercel merge, List enumerates
  local refs, optional AuthorReader). Reads resolve a ref → commit tree and use
  shared read helpers; writes build the subtree via the embedded *treeWriter.
- Share the tree-read helpers: the git-branch reader's Read/ReadSession* now
  delegate to readSummaryFromCheckpointTree / readSession*FromTree free functions

  tree differently.

  + gitRefsBackendFactory; OpenEnv/OpenOptions gain RefFetcher; PrimaryIsRefs helper.
- pushqueue.go: flock-protected JSONL push-discovery queue in the git common dir
  (Enqueue/Drain/Remove); gitRefsStore.setRef enqueues best-effort. (Pre-push
  consumption lands in the next commit.)
- CheckpointVersionRefsV1 = "refs-v1".

evidence.subject: Funnel all session-state mutations through MutateSessionState
evidence.body:
The previous PostToolUse-only lock fixed parallel PostToolUse races but
left every other writer (TurnEnd, PostCommit, condense, model update,
review env adoption, attribution divergence, post-rewrite remap, etc.)
doing its own unlocked load → mutate → save. A PostToolUse save could
still revert Phase, CheckpointTranscriptStart, TurnCheckpointIDs, token
usage, and other fields if it landed between another writer's load and
save.

Convert every session-state load-modify-save in the lifecycle dispatcher
and strategy package to MutateSessionState (or, for the rare new-state
case, to wrap the lone save in acquireSessionGate). The helper now:
  - Takes an OS flock against .git/entire-session-locks/<id>.lock for
    the duration of the load + fn + save.
  - Layers a per-process gate keyed by goroutine ID over the flock so
    nested calls in the same goroutine share the outer's state pointer
    rather than deadlocking on a second flock or losing inner updates
    to the outer save.
  - Returns ErrStateNotFound when no state file exists, letting callers
    distinguish "no session" from a successful no-op.
  - Honours ErrMutationSkip so fn can decline to save when the merge
    produced no change (key for the PostToolUse hot path).

Lock files moved out of .git/entire-sessions/ so callers that enumerate
session state (tests, doctor, status) don't have to filter them.
ClearSessionState sweeps the lock too.

Adds TestMutateSessionState_NestedCallsAreReentrant to lock in the
nested-cal

evidence.subject: Fix stale transcript in deferred condensation and add sentinel-based flush detection
evidence.body:
Two fixes for transcript reliability:

1. Condensation now prefers the live transcript file (state.TranscriptPath) over the
   shadow branch copy. When SaveChanges is skipped (no code changes on turn end),
   the shadow branch transcript becomes stale. Deferred condensation
   (ACTIVE_COMMITTED → IDLE) would read this stale copy, losing the entire last
   conversation turn. The live file is always current.

   Claude Code writes a hook_progress entry to the transcript when launching hooks.
   We poll for this entry to ensure the file is fully flushed before copying,
   preventing partial transcript reads.

evidence.subject: harden: address PR review — Windows volume + glob-metachar session IDs
evidence.body:
Three issues from PR #1365 review:

- ValidateSessionID accepted Windows drive-relative paths ("C:foo"):
  separator-free and not reported absolute by filepath.IsAbs, yet
  filepath.Join drops the base dir on a volume name. Reject ":" (the
  volume separator) — portable and testable; no legitimate session ID
  contains a colon.

- ValidateSessionID accepted glob metacharacters ("*", "?", "["). Session
  IDs are interpolated into filepath.Glob patterns (agent transcript
  lookup in gemini/pi/codex, session-state cleanup), so a "*" could match
  unrelated files. Reject them at the validator choke point.

- StateStore.Clear and ClearSessionState globbed "<sessionID>.*" to find
  files to DELETE. With the permissive validator a session ID of "*"
  would have matched and removed every session's state (DoS/data-loss
  within the state dir). Replace globbing with literal prefix matching so
  deletion can never depend on pattern interpretation, even if a future
  caller skips validation.

Adds regression tests for the drive-relative and glob-metacharacter cases.

evidence.subject: Funnel all session-state mutations through MutateSessionState
evidence.body:
The previous PostToolUse-only lock fixed parallel PostToolUse races but
left every other writer (TurnEnd, PostCommit, condense, model update,
review env adoption, attribution divergence, post-rewrite remap, etc.)
doing its own unlocked load → mutate → save. A PostToolUse save could
still revert Phase, CheckpointTranscriptStart, TurnCheckpointIDs, token
usage, and other fields if it landed between another writer's load and
save.

Convert every session-state load-modify-save in the lifecycle dispatcher
and strategy package to MutateSessionState (or, for the rare new-state
case, to wrap the lone save in acquireSessionGate). The helper now:
  - Takes an OS flock against .git/entire-session-locks/<id>.lock for
    the duration of the load + fn + save.
  - Layers a per-process gate keyed by goroutine ID over the flock so
    nested calls in the same goroutine share the outer's state pointer
    rather than deadlocking on a second flock or losing inner updates
    to the outer save.
  - Returns ErrStateNotFound when no state file exists, letting callers
    distinguish "no session" from a successful no-op.
  - Honours ErrMutationSkip so fn can decline to save when the merge
    produced no change (key for the PostToolUse hot path).

Lock files moved out of .git/entire-sessions/ so callers that enumerate
session state (tests, doctor, status) don't have to filter them.
ClearSessionState sweeps the lock too.

Adds TestMutateSessionState_NestedCallsAreReentrant to lock in the
nested-cal

Pins github.com/entireio/auth-go to its hardened OAuth client (PR #5
head), which validates Resource as an origin URL, refuses unsigned JWTs
(alg:none), enforces HTTPS unless the host is loopback, validates the
verification_uri returned by the AS, and centralises OAuth error
parsing with sanitised descriptions.

auth/client.go: now a thin shim over deviceflow.Client. Preserves the
historical DeviceAuthStart/DeviceAuthPoll types as aliases / equivalent
shapes so login.go's polling switch keeps working. Unknown OAuth error
codes are surfaced through DeviceAuthPoll.Error/ErrorDescription so
login.go can fail fast on terminal rejections instead of treating them
as transient.

auth/store.go: implements tokenstore.Store (SaveTokens/LoadTokens/
DeleteTokens) so it can be passed to tokenmanager.New. Adds a defensive
JSON-shape check on read — pre-shim entries are opaque token strings,
never JSON; a JSON blob in the keyring is corruption and must not be
put on the wire as a bearer.

auth/exchange.go: new package-level Manager wired from CurrentProvider,
AuthBaseURL, and NewStore. Exposes TokenForResource(ctx, url) and Token
(ctx, req); both go through the manager's same-host shortcut, JWT-aud
shortcut, and STS exchange dispatch as appropriate. SetManagerForTest()
takes a mutex so concurrent tests can swap without racing.

Single-host deployments hit the same-host shortcut and never call STS;
split-host deployments perform an RFC 8693 token exchange against the
auth issuer's STS endpoi

evidence.subject: Add `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints` (git-branch → git-refs)
evidence.body:
Convert checkpoints on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch into per-checkpoint refs
(refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>), the git-refs store's layout.

checkpoint.MigrateBranchToRefs walks the v1 branch tip and, for each checkpoint,
wraps its CURRENT subtree object in a fresh commit and points the ref at it —
existing branch commits are not remapped. Since the git-refs ref tree is the
branch's <shard>/<id> subtree byte-for-byte, a migrated checkpoint reads
identically under either backend. It is idempotent: a checkpoint whose ref
already carries the same tree is skipped, and a changed checkpoint re-migrates by
fast-forward (new commit parents on the existing ref, so no history is lost).
New/advanced refs are enqueued for push; the function itself never pushes.

The `doctor migrate-checkpoints` command reports migrated/skipped/total and, per
the requested policy, only pushes when it can prompt: interactively it asks
whether to push now; non-interactively it never pushes (refs stay queued and
flush on the next push once git-refs is primary). `--dry-run` reports what would
change without writing refs.

Push reuse: the git-refs pre-push queue-flush is extracted into
strategy.flushCheckpointRefsQueue (shared by the fail-soft pre-push path and the
new error-surfacing strategy.PushMigratedCheckpointRefs), so the "push now"
option goes through the exact same fast-forward + fetch/replay logic.

evidence.subject: Recover a diverged checkpoint ref by fetch+replay instead of leaving it queued
evidence.body:
Build on the non-force push: when a per-checkpoint ref is rejected (it diverged
on the remote — the same checkpoint re-written elsewhere), instead of just
leaving it queued, fetch the remote ref and replay the local-only commits on top
via the existing fetchAndRebaseRefCommon, then retry. The retry stays non-force
(after the replay the local ref is a fast-forward over the remote), so the
remote's commit is preserved as an ancestor, never overwritten. The cherry-pick
is delta-based, so non-overlapping changes merge; a genuine overlap (both sides
rewrote the same file) surfaces as a rebase error and the ref is left for a later
pre-push — degrading to the previous safe behavior, never to a force overwrite.

pre-push keeps the batch push as the fast path (one round-trip when everything
fast-forwards) and falls back to this per-ref recovery only for rejected refs,
removing from the queue just those that land. Adds a test proving a diverged ref
ends up with both the remote-only and local-only changes after recovery.

evidence.subject: git-refs: compact the push queue on Drain
evidence.body:
Enqueue only appends, so a long-lived session that re-enqueues the same
checkpoint ref across many writes without pushing would grow the queue file
unboundedly — Remove was the only point that rewrote it. Drain already
de-duplicates in memory; now it also rewrites the file to that de-duplicated set
when the on-disk queue held redundant lines (duplicate refs or malformed/blank
records), bounding the file to one line per distinct queued ref.

readLocked reports the raw non-empty line count so Drain compacts only when
rawLines > len(refs) (i.e. there was actually something redundant). The rewrite
is factored into rewriteLocked, shared with Remove, and stays atomic (temp +
rename). Drain still returns the refs and does not clear them — they survive
until a confirmed Remove.

evidence.body:
Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have
`entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code. A branch
checkout could then swap what ran. This repo shipped exactly that: `local_dev:
true` was tracked, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. Removed the `--local-dev` flags
(including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`,
the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and
the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and
the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented no-op: the loaders use
DisallowUnknownFields, so deleting the field would make every existing settings
file containing `local_dev` a hard parse error. It is not merged from overrides
and nothing reads it, matching the `Strategy` precedent.

Removing the feature is not enough to disarm existing installs, so this also
fixes how hooks written by older versions get replaced:

- `isGitHookInstalledInHooksDir` only looked for the Entire marker, which a

evidence.subject: Surface untrusted Codex hooks in the SessionStart welcome
evidence.body:
When entire ships a new hook (the recent PostToolUse addition is the
first instance, more will follow), users who trusted earlier versions
of our hooks won't have a \`trusted_hash\` entry for the new one in
their ~/.codex/config.toml. Codex's own startup warning catches this,
but it's generic — the user has to read the /hooks UI to figure out
which hook came from where.

Reaching the SessionStart hook handler proves SessionStart is itself
trusted, so it's the right place to add a contextual nudge: if any
other event we declared in .codex/hooks.json lacks a state entry under
the same hooks-file path, append a one-liner naming the missing events
to the welcome message.

Detection is structural — we read the user's config.toml and look for
\`[hooks.state."<hooks.json>:<event>:<group>:<handler>"]\` headers, no
hash recomputation. That misses the "command changed, hash mismatched"
case (status = Modified), but Codex's own warning still surfaces it,
so we don't need to. The check stays cheap and free of the brittle
hash-replication coupling we declined for production pre-trust.

Codex-only: other agents don't have a per-user trust gate.

evidence.subject: Serialize parallel PostToolUse writes with a per-session file lock
evidence.body:
Codex parallelizes tool calls, so multiple PostToolUse hook processes
can race the load → merge → save sequence in RecordFilesTouched. Without
serialization, two parallel apply_patch calls can lose each other's
FilesTouched merges (last writer wins on the whole state blob).

Wrap the critical section with an OS-level advisory lock against
.git/entire-sessions/<id>.lock — POSIX flock on Unix,
LockFileEx on Windows. Use a sibling .lock file rather than locking
the state file itself, since Save's atomic-rename pattern unlinks the
inode the flock would be held on. The .lock filename matches the
existing Clear() glob so cleanup paths still purge it.

Scope is intentionally narrow: only RecordFilesTouched participates in
the lock today. PostToolUse-vs-{TurnEnd,PostCommit} cross-handler races
remain (a stale RecordFilesTouched save can still revert fields those
handlers updated between our load and save), but the window is now
bounded by the load+save inside the lock rather than the full hook
subprocess duration. Full coverage will require converting all
session-state mutators to a shared MutateSessionState(ctx, fn) helper
— left as a follow-up.

evidence.subject: fix(redact): fail closed when OPF is enabled with no categories
evidence.body:
With openai_privacy_filter.enabled: true but an empty effective
category set (categories omitted, {}, or all-false), the model scan
never ran, yet the pre-push rewrite still stamped Entire-OPF-Applied:
true on every rebuilt commit. Later rewrites treat that trailer as
proof the commit was scanned and skip it permanently, so fixing the
config afterwards never repaired the falsely-attested commits, and
prose PII that only the model layer detects could reach the remote.

Fail closed instead, at two layers:

- RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF aborts with the new OPFNoCategoriesError
  sentinel before any commit is rebuilt, so no trailer is stamped and
  a corrected config scans the same commits on the next push. The
  check sits before the breaker check so the user gets config-specific
  remediation rather than 'verify your OPF install'.
- BatchBytesWithPrivacyFilter returns ErrOPFNoEnabledCategories for
  the enabled-with-zero-categories state instead of silently returning
  regex-only output, as defense in depth for its trailer-stamping
  caller. Unconfigured/disabled/breaker-tripped still return regex-only
  output with no error, unchanged.

deliberately NOT done: hooks swallow settings.Load errors
(EnsureRedactionConfigured logs and returns), so a Load-time rejection
would leave OPF unconfigured and let the push proceed regex-only with
no message at all — a silent unprotected push instead of a loud abort.

topology rule:

  through the repo and its refs). buildPrimary checks the capability instead of
  comparing against the literal "git".

  parallel-rollout topology — which the previous "no git-backed mirror" block
  would have forbidden.

A future per-mirror config (same type, distinct repo/refs) could relax the
one-of-each-type rule further.

evidence.subject: Add checkpoints backend selection settings and mirror fan-out
evidence.body:
Wire the registry to settings-driven backend selection and add independent
backend mirroring.

Settings: a new `checkpoints.{primary, mirrors}` block using a discriminated
{type, config} shape, read through a dedicated lenient loader
(settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig). The loader is fail-soft by design — a missing
file, whole-file JSON syntax error, or unrelated invalid settings all resolve
to "no config" so checkpoint construction defaults to git; it errors only when
a present `checkpoints` block is itself invalid. This avoids making Open newly
fail on unrelated malformed settings (the strict settings.Load path still
surfaces those for normal commands). The field also lives on EntireSettings so
the strict loader accepts a `checkpoints` key.

Open: builds the primary and mirrors through the registry. The primary must be
git (attach/resume/push/doctor/cleanup/OPF all assume a git refs.Primary), so a
non-git primary is rejected. A git-typed mirror is rejected too: it would share
the primary ref topology and double-write the same ref.

fanoutStore: serves all reads from the primary and writes to the primary first,
then fans out best-effort to each mirror (failures logged, never surfaced).
With no mirrors it returns the primary unwrapped, preserving its concrete type
and optional capabilities. When wrapping, it preserves the optional AuthorReader
iff the primary implements it, so explain's author fallback keeps working.

subagent tracking, even though it ships first-class hooks for it. Wire them.

layout to guess, add Event.SubagentTranscriptPath so an agent can *declare* where
its subagent transcript is; handleLifecycleSubagentEnd prefers it and falls back to
the Claude Code layout guess. A declared-but-missing path warns rather than
silently substituting, because that disagreement is exactly what went unnoticed
while the guess quietly returned "" for every non-Claude agent.

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**

evidence.subject: feat(codex): track subagents via Codex's SubagentStart/SubagentStop hooks
evidence.body:
Codex was the one agent named in the original subagent-tracking request with zero
subagent tracking, even though it ships first-class hooks for it. Wire them.

Codex's identity fields are the opposite of what the names suggest, and getting
this backwards would attribute subagent work to a session Entire has never seen:

  - session_id is "the identity shared by the root thread and all descendant
    threads" (session/session.rs) — the *user's* session. It maps straight to
    SessionID.
  - agent_id is the subagent thread's own id. Codex sends no tool_use_id, so
    agent_id doubles as ToolUseID: it is the only value correlating a start with
    its stop, and Entire keys pre-task state (pre-task-<id>.json) and the task
    metadata directory on ToolUseID.

SubagentStop also carries two transcripts — transcript_path is the parent rollout,
agent_transcript_path the subagent's own. Rather than teach the framework a second
layout to guess, add Event.SubagentTranscriptPath so an agent can *declare* where
its subagent transcript is; handleLifecycleSubagentEnd prefers it and falls back to
the Claude Code layout guess. A declared-but-missing path warns rather than
silently substituting, because that disagreement is exactly what went unnoticed
while the guess quietly returned "" for every non-Claude agent.

That mechanism immediately fixes a second agent: Cursor has parsed
agent_transcript_path into its raw struct all along and never forwarded it, so
Cursor fell back to probing Claude

and batch force-pushes those per-checkpoint refs (one git push, +ref:ref force

evidence.subject: fix(strategy): defer checkpoint push until a normal remote branch exists (#1743)
evidence.body:
When Entire is enabled before a repository has any branch on its remote,
the pre-push hook could independently publish entire/checkpoints/v1 ahead
of the user's first normal branch. On an empty GitHub repo that metadata
branch can become the repository default branch.

Route the Git pre-push hook through a new PrePushFromGitHook that, for the
user's push remote, inspects the actual push target(s) (including a
distinct pushurl via `git remote get-url --push --all`) and defers
automatic checkpoint publication until a non-metadata branch exists there.

evidence.subject: Add `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints` (git-branch → git-refs)
evidence.body:
Convert checkpoints on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch into per-checkpoint refs
(refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>), the git-refs store's layout.

checkpoint.MigrateBranchToRefs walks the v1 branch tip and, for each checkpoint,
wraps its CURRENT subtree object in a fresh commit and points the ref at it —
existing branch commits are not remapped. Since the git-refs ref tree is the
branch's <shard>/<id> subtree byte-for-byte, a migrated checkpoint reads
identically under either backend. It is idempotent: a checkpoint whose ref
already carries the same tree is skipped, and a changed checkpoint re-migrates by
fast-forward (new commit parents on the existing ref, so no history is lost).
New/advanced refs are enqueued for push; the function itself never pushes.

The `doctor migrate-checkpoints` command reports migrated/skipped/total and, per
the requested policy, only pushes when it can prompt: interactively it asks
whether to push now; non-interactively it never pushes (refs stay queued and
flush on the next push once git-refs is primary). `--dry-run` reports what would
change without writing refs.

Push reuse: the git-refs pre-push queue-flush is extracted into
strategy.flushCheckpointRefsQueue (shared by the fail-soft pre-push path and the
new error-surfacing strategy.PushMigratedCheckpointRefs), so the "push now"
option goes through the exact same fast-forward + fetch/replay logic.

evidence.body:
Committed checkpoint writes now generate a compact transcript
(transcript.jsonl) from the full transcript via transcript/compact and
store it in the session directory next to full.jsonl, so it is pushed
with the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch. The root metadata.json
sessions[].transcript pointer targets transcript.jsonl when it was
generated and falls back to full.jsonl otherwise (unparseable or
external-agent transcripts, checkpoints from older CLI versions).

Unlike the removed v2 (cumulative compact plus compact-unit offset),
the stored compact is pre-sliced to the checkpoint's own portion:
compact.Compact runs with StartLine = checkpoint_transcript_start.
v1's checkpoint_transcript_start must keep full.jsonl units for CLI
readers, so a pre-sliced file avoids a new offset field and is
self-describing for consumers. Generation is best-effort and never
fails the checkpoint write; finalization (UpdateCommitted) regenerates
the compact from the new content and keeps the previous one on
generation failure so the metadata pointer never dangles. CLI read
paths (rewind/resume/explain) are unaffected: they read full.jsonl by
filename, not through the metadata pointer.

evidence.subject: compact: add FullWithBoundary for full transcript + scope marker
evidence.body:
FullWithBoundary compacts the entire transcript (ignoring StartLine for
truncation) and returns the full compact bytes plus the line index at which
this checkpoint's slice begins in the compact output. The boundary is derived
as lineCount(full) - lineCount(delta), reusing each format's existing,
independently-tested slicing behavior rather than threading source indices
through all seven emitters. The only imprecision is a deterministic off-by-one
when a single logical message straddles the exact boundary.

This is the foundation for storing a full, self-contained compact transcript on
every checkpoint (so a session is reconstructable from any single checkpoint)
while still letting readers segment a checkpoint's slice via the marker.

re-redacted it from byte zero. On a 70MB Codex rollout that was ~67s per Stop

appended. Two properties make the splice sound:

Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have

but nothing enforced it: `LegacyLocalDevHookScript` was exported, so any agent

byte-identical and claudecode differed only in resolving the repo root through

ours regardless of whose config it appears in, and a newly added agent inherits
legacy detection instead of having to remember to copy the list — omitting those
entries is exactly what leaves an old hook installed forever.

checkpoint store with a bounded ref fetcher and no blob fetcher. On a partial
clone that is not enough: the ref resolves, then the checkpoint's own
metadata.json is a filtered-out blob, and GitStore.Read maps an unreadable
metadata.json to (nil, nil) — "checkpoint not found". Attribution is skipped
and the finalized transcript never reaches its checkpoints, with nothing above
Debug to say why.

Until #2141 those reads were rescued by git's own promisor fetch inside
`cat-file`, unbounded and one round-trip per blob, from inside a hook the
user's git command was waiting on. Disabling that was right; leaving the paths
with no way to fetch was not.

Give them the same envelope the ref probe there already has: the write-probe
budget over the whole call plus BatchMode SSH, so a passphrase-protected key
cannot prompt or hang. Both bounds now come from one
hookCheckpointStoreOptions, because a hook with one and not the other still
reports checkpoints that exist as missing. The fetcher fires only when a blob
is genuinely absent locally, so a full clone never pays for it.

Not addressed here, deliberately: head_checkpoint_flags and review_context
read fetcher-less too, but they feed `entire status` and review context
enrichment, where a network fetch is worse than the missing hint;
dispatch/mode_local needs the fetcher plumbed across a package boundary; and
explain's temporary-checkpoint store reads the shadow

evidence.subject: Add `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints` (git-branch → git-refs)
evidence.body:
Convert checkpoints on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch into per-checkpoint refs
(refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>), the git-refs store's layout.

checkpoint.MigrateBranchToRefs walks the v1 branch tip and, for each checkpoint,
wraps its CURRENT subtree object in a fresh commit and points the ref at it —
existing branch commits are not remapped. Since the git-refs ref tree is the
branch's <shard>/<id> subtree byte-for-byte, a migrated checkpoint reads
identically under either backend. It is idempotent: a checkpoint whose ref
already carries the same tree is skipped, and a changed checkpoint re-migrates by
fast-forward (new commit parents on the existing ref, so no history is lost).
New/advanced refs are enqueued for push; the function itself never pushes.

The `doctor migrate-checkpoints` command reports migrated/skipped/total and, per
the requested policy, only pushes when it can prompt: interactively it asks
whether to push now; non-interactively it never pushes (refs stay queued and
flush on the next push once git-refs is primary). `--dry-run` reports what would
change without writing refs.

Push reuse: the git-refs pre-push queue-flush is extracted into
strategy.flushCheckpointRefsQueue (shared by the fail-soft pre-push path and the
new error-surfacing strategy.PushMigratedCheckpointRefs), so the "push now"
option goes through the exact same fast-forward + fetch/replay logic.

evidence.subject: migrate: re-enqueue already-imported refs so a lost enqueue still pushes
evidence.body:
The idempotency skip keyed only on "snapshot already on the ref," so a
ref written by a prior run that then failed to enqueue it — an Enqueue
error, or a crash between setRef and Enqueue — was skipped on every
later run and never queued for push. The migrated ref then existed
locally but its checkpoint data never reached the remote, silently
defeating the guaranteed-enqueue contract on exactly the retry it was
meant to enable.

Compute the ref name up front and enqueue on the skip path too (never in
dry-run). Enqueue is idempotent — duplicates collapse on Drain and an
already-pushed ref is a no-op on the next push — so re-enqueuing a
skipped checkpoint is safe and closes the gap. Dry-run now accounts an
already-imported checkpoint as a skip rather than reaching the old
would-migrate branch, and writes/enqueues nothing.

evidence.subject: fix(explain): recover the v1 metadata branch from the checkpoint remote
evidence.body:
A fresh clone of a repo whose checkpoints live on a dedicated
checkpoint_remote could not read any legacy hex-ID checkpoint. The
git-branch store resolved reads from the local v1 ref, then from origin's
remote-tracking ref, then gave up — and a checkpoint_remote setup has
neither, because the branch was never pushed to origin. `entire explain
<hex-id>` reported the checkpoint as unreadable with no way to recover.

Add a third tier: MetadataBranchFetchFunc, the git-branch counterpart to
the git-refs store's RefFetchFunc. Where that store resolves one missing
per-checkpoint ref, this one resolves the single branch the whole record
lives on. It is injected from the CLI layer like the other fetchers, so
the checkpoint package still resolves no remotes itself.

The tier is recovery, not refresh: it fires only when the branch resolves
neither locally nor from origin, so a normal read stays local and the hot
paths — which do not wire a fetcher at all — stay network-free. A failed
fetch leaves the original not-found error intact, keeping List's
offline-reads-as-empty behavior.

Wired into explain's read paths only. resume already self-heals through
its own fetch ladder; the remaining callers are hooks and background
paths where a network call on read would be wrong.

evidence.subject: migrate: --dry-run no longer writes loose git objects
evidence.body:
migratedCheckpointTree ran before the dry-run guard and, for any
checkpoint whose metadata needs normalizing, called CreateBlobFromContent
+ ApplyTreeChanges — both persist via SetEncodedObject. So a "preview"
that promises to report "without writing" left a dangling blob + tree per
checkpoint in the object store (thousands on a large v1 branch, until a
future git gc).

Thread the dry-run flag into migratedCheckpointTree: when not persisting,
compute the normalized blob and tree hashes in memory (git hashes are
content-addressed, so an object encoded but not stored hashes identically
to a persisted one) and return without touching the object store. The
persisting path is unchanged. A new test asserts the object count is
unchanged across a dry-run, and another migrates for real then dry-runs
again and asserts the checkpoint is recognized as already-migrated —
pinning the in-memory hash to the persisted tree hash.

title: auth-go lock dir isolation doesn't cover spawned binaries

evidence.subject: tests: never touch the user's real config, cache, or keychain
evidence.body:
A test fixture (bob@core.example.com) leaked into a developer's real
~/.config/entire/contexts.json. Unit tests isolated config access only
by per-test convention (t.Setenv), and the integration/e2e harnesses
spawned the real entire binary with the developer's real environment —
no ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR, no XDG_CACHE_HOME, real HOME, real OS keychain.

Defense in depth:

- internal/testdirs (new): under `go test`, resolution of the config
  dir, cache dir, and token store falls back to a throwaway per-process
  temp directory when the explicit env override is unset, so an
  unisolated test can never read or write real user state.
- Wired into contexts.DefaultConfigDir, discovery.DefaultCacheDir,
  versioncheck, and the tokenstore default backend (which previously
  defaulted to the real OS keyring even under test).
- versioncheck now honors ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR before falling back to
  ~/.config/entire, so one env var isolates every config-dir surface.
- Integration and e2e TestMains export ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR,
  XDG_CACHE_HOME, and file-backed token-store env vars process-wide;
  spawned binaries (where testing.Testing() is false) inherit them
  through every os.Environ()-based env builder.
- CLAUDE.md documents the isolation rules for future harnesses.

evidence.subject: fix(auth): name the context and core when a login server is unreachable
evidence.body:
A context left pointing at a core that is no longer listening — a local
dev core, typically — failed with nothing a user could act on:

  refresh login token: refresh token: Post "https://localhost:8180/oauth/token":
  dial tcp [::1]:8180: connect: connection refused

Neither the context that chose that host nor a command that fixes it
appeared anywhere. It now reads:

  cannot reach the login server for "local" (https://localhost:8180): dial
  tcp [::1]:8180: connect: connection refused; run `entire login` to sign in
  again, or `entire auth use <context>` to switch to another login

The two re-auth sentinels already got this treatment; transport failures
fell through to a generic wrap. contextReauthError becomes contextAuthError
and ends with the new mapper, so both the login-JWT path and the STS
exchange path route through one place.

Gated on *url.Error: a 4xx from the token endpoint is a credential problem,

title: Make test git isolation structural: runGit helper + forbidigo rule

evidence.subject: Rewrite relative alternates so go-git can follow shared clones
evidence.body:
go-git's dotgit.Alternates() strips leading "../" and anchors entries at
the filesystem root, so relative objects/info/alternates entries — the
shape produced by `git clone --shared`/`--reference` — point at
non-existent paths. The pre-push checkpoint sync then fails to resolve
alternate-resident commits even though git itself reads them.

Wrap both the dotgit and common-git filesystems with an alternates
rewriter that resolves relative entries against <root>/objects on read.
The rewriter preserves file structure (comments, blanks, absolute
entries pass through untouched), caps reads at 4096 bytes, and applies
to nested alternate chains via the os-rooted AlternatesFS. Linked
worktrees are covered because the wrap applies to the common dir where
the alternates file actually lives.

Adds unit tests for the rewriter, integration tests for OpenPath across
multiple/nested/linked-worktree relative-alternate layouts, and an e2e
test reproducing the shared-clone checkpoint sync failure. Tests that
shell out to git get GIT_CONFIG_* isolation so they don't pick up host
config.

evidence.subject: refactor(hooks)!: remove local_dev mode
evidence.body:
Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have
`entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code. A branch
checkout could then swap what ran. This repo shipped exactly that: `local_dev:
true` was tracked, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. Removed the `--local-dev` flags
(including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`,
the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and
the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and
the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented no-op: the loaders use
DisallowUnknownFields, so deleting the field would make every existing settings
file containing `local_dev` a hard parse error. It is not merged from overrides
and nothing reads it, matching the `Strategy` precedent.

Removing the feature is not enough to disarm existing installs, so this also
fixes how hooks written by older versions get replaced:

configs are committed files that turn up in a diff; git hooks are per-clone and

evidence.subject: feat(enable)!: take history import out of --yes, behind an explicit --import-history
evidence.body:
`--yes` means "accept all defaults", and the interactive import default is
to import nothing — the multi-select pre-checks nothing, so pressing
enter through it skips. Implying an import from --yes therefore made the
unattended path do the opposite of the attended one.

It also let a single flag carry two unrelated decisions. In a non-repo
directory `--yes` already means "init git, create a private GitHub repo,
commit, and push"; folding history import in meant one flag both created
a remote and ingested a month of local transcripts destined for it.
Publishing existing agent history is its own decision.

`--import-history` is now the non-interactive way to say yes. `--yes`
takes the same path as any other run that makes no choice: import
nothing, point at `entire import <agent>`. The flag is first-run only,
like the offer it drives, and says so when it cannot apply rather than
being silently dropped.

BREAKING CHANGE: `entire enable --yes` no longer imports pre-existing
agent history. Pass --import-history, or run `entire import <agent>`.

evidence.subject: feat(strategy): capture the checkpoint sync remote from tracked pushes
evidence.body:
The single-remote election (ENT-1451) guesses the sync destination from
config at rest — origin, else sole, else first in .git/config — so a user
whose branches push a non-origin remote had checkpoints strand locally
until they hand-configured checkpoint_push_remote. First user report
landed the day after v0.10.0 shipped.

Capture makes the election follow demonstrated push behavior with zero
configuration: during pre-push, a push whose target agrees with the
branch's declared push destination (branch.<name>.pushRemote ->
remote.pushDefault -> branch.<name>.remote — the config a bare
'git push' resolves through) and differs from the current election
persists that remote as the captured election, announces it on stderr,
and the same push carries the checkpoints. The captured tier sits
between the explicit setting and origin, and is fail-soft: a captured
remote that was renamed or removed falls through to the default tiers
instead of disabling sync.

Neither signal elects alone. Declaration without a push is the
config-at-rest bug that got the static tracking tier dropped (74e239a9:
a 'clone -o base' stranded every origin push); a push without
declaration is the pre-single-remote transcript leak (a one-off
'git push upstream' must never publish transcripts). Capture acts only
on their intersection.

Phase-1 rules: at most one captured remote and the first capture sticks,
so a mixed-habit repo whose branches push two remotes cannot flip the
election on every push. The state file

evidence.subject: fix(strategy): scope empty-remote guard to configured remotes; document staleness limit
evidence.body:
Addresses two trail-review findings on the local-ref guard:

- URL-push defers forever (fix): git hands the pre-push hook the bare URL as
  the remote arg when a push targets a URL directly (verified: $1 is the URL,
  not a name). git never records refs/remotes/<url>/*, so remoteHasTrackingRefs
  was always false → checkpoints deferred permanently for URL-push workflows.
  Guard now runs only when the arg resolves to a configured remote
  (isConfiguredRemote via `git remote get-url`, local/no-network); a bare-URL
  target publishes instead of stranding metadata. The first-branch hazard the
  guard exists for always uses a named remote, so no protection is lost. This
  also matches the reviewer's "…or default to origin" note.

- Recreated-empty-remote staleness (documented): a tracking ref left from before
  a remote was deleted and recreated empty under the same URL reads as
  "established", so v1 could publish to the now-empty remote. Detecting that
  needs a network round trip, which this design deliberately avoids; the earlier
  TTL only bounded a network probe's cache and no longer applies. Rare and
  recoverable — noted inline as an accepted limitation rather than reintroducing
  the network hit.

Test adds a bare-URL case asserting the guard publishes (does not defer).

evidence.body:
Bound the sweep's condensing. Widening OwnerExited to IDLE multiplied the
candidate set — IDLE is the resting state, so the sweep now catches every agent
quit at its prompt, not just ones killed mid-turn — and each candidate triggered
a deadline-free condense inside `entire status`. Measured, one condense is
~120ms floor and seconds for a real transcript, against a 40ms command, serially
and uncapped; with a 7-day StaleSessionThreshold the first sweep after upgrade
drains a week's backlog in one stall, and `--json` (the MCP entire_status tool)
prints nothing until it finishes. sweepCondenseBudget now caps condensing across
the whole sweep while every candidate is still marked ENDED, which is what
actually un-sticks it from `entire status`. A new test pins that split.

- Hoist the "already finalized" rule to State.IsEnded(); it was spelled out at

  over one sessionInfoRaw, matching geminicli and factoryaidroid, which solved

evidence.subject: Funnel all session-state mutations through MutateSessionState
evidence.body:
The previous PostToolUse-only lock fixed parallel PostToolUse races but
left every other writer (TurnEnd, PostCommit, condense, model update,
review env adoption, attribution divergence, post-rewrite remap, etc.)
doing its own unlocked load → mutate → save. A PostToolUse save could
still revert Phase, CheckpointTranscriptStart, TurnCheckpointIDs, token
usage, and other fields if it landed between another writer's load and
save.

Convert every session-state load-modify-save in the lifecycle dispatcher
and strategy package to MutateSessionState (or, for the rare new-state
case, to wrap the lone save in acquireSessionGate). The helper now:
  - Takes an OS flock against .git/entire-session-locks/<id>.lock for
    the duration of the load + fn + save.
  - Layers a per-process gate keyed by goroutine ID over the flock so
    nested calls in the same goroutine share the outer's state pointer
    rather than deadlocking on a second flock or losing inner updates
    to the outer save.
  - Returns ErrStateNotFound when no state file exists, letting callers
    distinguish "no session" from a successful no-op.
  - Honours ErrMutationSkip so fn can decline to save when the merge
    produced no change (key for the PostToolUse hot path).

Lock files moved out of .git/entire-sessions/ so callers that enumerate
session state (tests, doctor, status) don't have to filter them.
ClearSessionState sweeps the lock too.

Adds TestMutateSessionState_NestedCallsAreReentrant to lock in the
nested-cal

evidence.subject: Add `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints` (git-branch → git-refs)
evidence.body:
Convert checkpoints on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch into per-checkpoint refs
(refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>), the git-refs store's layout.

checkpoint.MigrateBranchToRefs walks the v1 branch tip and, for each checkpoint,
wraps its CURRENT subtree object in a fresh commit and points the ref at it —
existing branch commits are not remapped. Since the git-refs ref tree is the
branch's <shard>/<id> subtree byte-for-byte, a migrated checkpoint reads
identically under either backend. It is idempotent: a checkpoint whose ref
already carries the same tree is skipped, and a changed checkpoint re-migrates by
fast-forward (new commit parents on the existing ref, so no history is lost).
New/advanced refs are enqueued for push; the function itself never pushes.

The `doctor migrate-checkpoints` command reports migrated/skipped/total and, per
the requested policy, only pushes when it can prompt: interactively it asks
whether to push now; non-interactively it never pushes (refs stay queued and
flush on the next push once git-refs is primary). `--dry-run` reports what would
change without writing refs.

Push reuse: the git-refs pre-push queue-flush is extracted into
strategy.flushCheckpointRefsQueue (shared by the fail-soft pre-push path and the
new error-surfacing strategy.PushMigratedCheckpointRefs), so the "push now"
option goes through the exact same fast-forward + fetch/replay logic.

error instead of a bool so each caller reports failure its own way: the
pre-push hook warns and continues, because a checkpoint failure must
never block the user's git push, while this push was explicitly
requested and so errors with the refs left queued, matching how it
already handles a blocking checkpoint policy. The next `git push`
applies OPF and delivers them.

pre-push rewrite and is unaffected.

evidence.subject: refactor(hooks)!: remove local_dev mode
evidence.body:
Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have
`entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code. A branch
checkout could then swap what ran. This repo shipped exactly that: `local_dev:
true` was tracked, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. Removed the `--local-dev` flags
(including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`,
the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and
the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and
the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented no-op: the loaders use

evidence.subject: feat(doctor): check and repair stale git hooks
evidence.body:
`.git/hooks` is the one hook surface a user cannot see going wrong. Agent hook
configs are committed files that turn up in a diff; git hooks are per-clone and
untracked, so pulling a release that changes hook generation never touches them.
A hook left by the removed local-dev mode still carries Entire's marker, so it
looks installed while naming a launcher inside the working tree that is gone —
and because that shape got no availability guard while pre-push propagates exit
codes, the symptom is `git push` being rejected. Doctor had no git-hook check at
all, so the place a user looks after a rejected push said nothing.

Unlike the sibling agent hook checks this one repairs rather than only warning:
the reinstall is content-idempotent, backs up any foreign hook it displaces, and
writes exactly what the next turn-start would write anyway. It degrades to
warn-only when there is nobody to ask, naming `--force` instead — doctor is a
diagnostic an agent or CI job runs unattended, so it must neither block on a
confirm nor rewrite a repo's hooks unasked. An existing bare-`doctor` test caught
that: without the guard the prompt fails to open a TTY and doctor exits 1.

adds strategy.GitHookState (Absent/Current/Outdated), mirroring
agent.HookConfigState so both hook surfaces share one vocabulary.

The `mirror list` stderr banner re-derived its core via
ResolveControlPlaneTarget, which ignores ENTIRE_TOKEN. In env-token mode
the request instead dials the token's own aud, so with both ENTIRE_TOKEN
and a contexts.json present the banner named a core the request never
talks to. The precedence (env-token-then-active-context) lives only inside
coreapi.New, and the client hid its resolved core, so every "talking to X"
display site was forced to re-derive it and could get it wrong.

Add coreapi.Client.CoreOrigin() — the single source of truth for "which
core am I dialing", reporting whatever was wired in (active context,

list banner from the live client's CoreOrigin so it can never diverge from
the request; this also makes it correct (rather than suppressed) in
env-token mode.

coreapi, so it now applies the env-token-first precedence and reports the
env token's core + bearer instead of a stale active context. logout stays
on the active context: it manages a stored session, which an env token lacks.

Extract auth.ParseEnvToken as the single owner of the ENTIRE_TOKEN
trim/blank/aud-validation sequence, shared by coreapi.New's bypass and
auth status (was duplicated inline in both).

evidence.subject: refactor(auth): require the active context, dropping implicit login selection
evidence.body:
Account selection had three tiers: the active context when the resource
trusted its core, else "the sole eligible context", else an ambiguity
error. The two implicit tiers are removed — the active context is the
identity, or the command fails.

The tiers made the acting identity depend on what *else* happened to be
stored. Adding a second login could silently change which account an
existing command ran as, and the same command could act as different
identities on two machines. Concretely: log into prod as alice, add a
staging login as admin for one task, and `git push` to a staging-fronted
cluster would authenticate as admin — an elevated account, with the
server-side audit trail recording it, and nothing in the output saying
so. For "whose credentials is this running under?", a predictable error
beats a convenient guess.

Multiple saved logins remain fully supported; `auth contexts`, `auth use`,
and `logout --all-contexts` are unchanged. What changes is that switching
is explicit.

Because "not logged in" is actively misleading for someone who IS logged
in, just to another federation, the failure now distinguishes what the
user can do about it: name the saved logins that would work and point at
`auth use`, or name the servers the resource trusts and point at
`entire login --server <url>`. That cashes in renderLoginHint's dead

absolute entries. Go's own protections do not reach the external-agent scanner:
it resolves by filepath.Glob, so a match never passes exec.LookPath (no ErrDot)
and it carries separators, so exec.Command's re-check does not apply either --

rule separately, which is how the two drifted; one helper keeps them aligned.

cmd.Dir to the worktree root and os/exec resolves a relative Path against Dir,
so the file registerExternalAgent statted is not necessarily the file that

evidence.subject: fix(git): validate branch names in the three helpers that skipped it
evidence.body:
BranchExistsOnRemote passes the name to `git ls-remote` and to go-git,
BranchExistsLocally to go-git, and CheckoutBranch to `git checkout` behind
nothing but a leading-dash guard. All three take names from CLI input or
from a trail's branch field.

The dash guard was the narrowest part of the problem: `git checkout` also
reads `--`, a pathspec, and `@{-1}`. ValidateBranchName covers those, and
it still admits an object id, so CheckoutBranch's documented "or commit"
behaviour survives even though no caller uses it.

Validating both existence helpers rather than only the remote one keeps
their answers symmetric: they are called side by side on the same name,
and "invalid" from one with "no such branch" from the other is worse than
either.

evidence.subject: session: resolve the session running the command, not the one that moved last
evidence.body:
`entire session current` answered "which session state moved most recently, preferring this worktree" and described it as "the active session for the current worktree". Worktrees share one session store, so in a worktree with no sessions of its own it silently fell back across the whole store and returned a live session belonging to somewhere else — that worktree's path right there in the JSON, indistinguishable from a real answer.

That is not a cosmetic mislabel. Agents reach for this command to find their own session id, read the id back, and pass it to `entire session adopt`, which moves the named session into the current worktree and resets its checkpoint bookkeeping. A wrong id there mutates a third party's running session.

Five agents already publish their session id into the environment of the processes they spawn, and Entire read none of them. `strategy.ResolveCallerSession` now answers the question directly, in tiers, each reported back so a caller can tell an identification from a guess: `caller-env` (the agent named it), `ancestry` (a session's recorded Owner is our ancestor — the same match commit linking performs, which is what covers the agents that publish nothing), `worktree`, then `other-worktree`. The weak tiers stay, because "what has been happening in this repo" is a real question; they just have to say that is what they answered. `SessionResolution.IsCaller()` is the gate for acting on a session rather than displaying it.

evidence.subject: proclive: add process-liveness package
evidence.body:
New leaf package that captures a process's identity (PID + start-time
fingerprint, plus host/boot guards) and reports whether that exact
process is still alive. ResolveOwner walks up the process tree to the
first non-shell, non-entire ancestor (the agent that spawned our hook),
skipping the Go toolchain too so local-dev's `go run` wrapper isn't
mistaken for the owner; it records no owner at all when the hostname
can't be determined, since a PID is only meaningful on its own machine.

Check returns Alive/Dead/Unknown — Dead on a missing PID, start-time
mismatch (PID reuse), or reboot, and Unknown when it can't confirm the
host/boot or the platform can't introspect (Windows), so callers fail
closed to a timeout rather than trusting a stale PID. darwin records no
boot guard: kern.boottime drifts when the wall clock is stepped (NTP),
and darwin's absolute P_starttime already distinguishes a reused PID
across reboots; Linux uses ticks-since-boot and keeps the boot_id guard.

Stdlib + golang.org/x/sys/unix only, so session/strategy/cli can import
it without an import cycle.

evidence.subject: feat(strategy): link commits to sessions by process identity
evidence.body:
Commit-to-session linking guessed by worktree path: the commit hooks
matched SessionState.WorktreePath against the commit's worktree. Any
drift between that bookkeeping and reality lost the linkage — an agent
committing in a sibling worktree produced an unlinked commit, or worse:
with a poisoned state dir, a wrong link. Both happened for real (three
retro-attach incidents; most recently a leaked test fixture session,
sessC, was linked to a commit and stamped a dangling trailer whose
checkpoint was never written).

Identity-first linking removes the guessing for agent commits. At
session start the hook records its nearest process ancestors
(pid + start time; the agent process is among them, since agents run
hooks as children) in SessionState.AgentAncestry. At commit time the
hook walks its own ancestry (git <- tool shell <- agent) and matches
those refs: nearest ancestor wins, ties go to the most recently
interacting session, start times guard against PID reuse. The identity
match is UNIONED with the worktree-matched set, never a replacement —
a commit condenses every session with pending content in its worktree,
and identity adds the one that path matching missed.

A commit identity-matched outside the session's home worktree is
guest-linked: condensed and linked, but worktree-coupled state
(BaseCommit, shadow-branch realignment) is never mutated from a foreign
worktree — shadow branches are keyed by BaseCommit + WorktreeID, and
the session's next home commit must still match

evidence.subject: Surface untrusted Codex hooks in the SessionStart welcome
evidence.body:
When entire ships a new hook (the recent PostToolUse addition is the
first instance, more will follow), users who trusted earlier versions
of our hooks won't have a \`trusted_hash\` entry for the new one in
their ~/.codex/config.toml. Codex's own startup warning catches this,
but it's generic — the user has to read the /hooks UI to figure out
which hook came from where.

Reaching the SessionStart hook handler proves SessionStart is itself
trusted, so it's the right place to add a contextual nudge: if any
other event we declared in .codex/hooks.json lacks a state entry under
the same hooks-file path, append a one-liner naming the missing events
to the welcome message.

Detection is structural — we read the user's config.toml and look for
\`[hooks.state."<hooks.json>:<event>:<group>:<handler>"]\` headers, no
hash recomputation. That misses the "command changed, hash mismatched"
case (status = Modified), but Codex's own warning still surfaces it,
so we don't need to. The check stays cheap and free of the brittle
hash-replication coupling we declined for production pre-trust.

Codex-only: other agents don't have a per-user trust gate.

evidence.subject: Don't --unshallow on push hot path: it's a global op, not ref-scoped
evidence.body:
git's --unshallow removes ALL shallow boundaries in .git/shallow, not
just the one for the ref being fetched. On a shallow clone of a large
repo it pulls the entire repository history (we observed 687 MB on
entirehq/entire). Used from the push hook, this hangs every push on
shallow repos until the full clone arrives.

The downstream reconcile/rebase paths already respect .git/shallow
(collectCommitChain stops at shallow boundaries; collectCommitsSince
uses git rev-list which respects them natively). When the local view
is shallow-truncated, the merge-base check may report "disconnected"
where the actual chains share ancestry below the boundary — but the
cherry-pick path it routes through still produces a correct result,
because it picks up exactly the commits that aren't yet on the remote.

Remove Unshallow from:
  - fetchAndRebaseSessionsCommon (push hot path)
  - FetchMetadataBranch (resume/explain fallback — only needs blobs)
  - FetchV2MainRef (same)

Keep Unshallow on metadata_reconcile's doctor v2 disconnection check
since it's only reached from `entire doctor`, an explicit
user-invoked diagnostic where the cost is acceptable.

Verified by re-running the full unit suite (5304 tests) and the
fetch-flag regression coverage from TestFetch_Unshallow /
TestFetch_Shallow.
